extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and scholars preparing notes and bibliographies (academic and professional writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for citing a wide variety of source types in notes and bibliographies, covering social media, interviews, manuscripts, archival materials, reference works, art, maps, scriptural and classical texts, and more. Focused on form, necessary elements, and when items belong in notes versus bibliographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain copies of cited social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Because social media content is subject to editing and deletion, authors are advised to retain a copy of anything they cite (see 14.15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save or archive social-media posts you cite; consult additional considerations in 14.6–18.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing electronic mailing lists and forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the name of the correspondent, the title of the subject or thread (in quotation marks and capitalized as in the original), the title of the list or forum (followed by list or forum or the like, if not part of the title), the title of any host site, the date of the message or post, and a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat posts on private forums or lists like personal communications (see 14.214).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished interviews citation form
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished interviews are best cited in text or in notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations should include the names of both the person interviewed and the interviewer; brief identifying information if appropriate; the place or date of the interview (or both, if known); and, if a transcript or recording is available, where it may be found. Permission to quote may be needed (see chapter 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unattributed (anonymous) interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: An interview with a person who prefers to remain anonymous or whose name the author does not wish to reveal may be cited in whatever form is appropriate in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain absence of a name (e.g., “All interviews were conducted in confidentiality, and the names of interviewees are withheld by mutual agreement”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Published or broadcast interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: An interview that has been published or broadcast or made available online can usually be treated like an article or other item in a periodical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews consulted online should include a URL or similar identifier (see 14.6–18); see also specific examples (14.264, 14.267).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal communications citation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: References to conversations (face-to-face or by telephone) or to letters, email or text messages, or direct/private messages received by the author are usually run into the text or given in a note and are rarely listed in a bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most such information can be referred to simply as a conversation, message, or the like; the medium may be mentioned if relevant. Omit an individual's email address unless permission is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation of theses and dissertations
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of theses and dissertations appear in quotation marks—not in italics; otherwise they are cited like books. The kind of thesis, the academic institution, and the date follow the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In notes these facts are enclosed in parentheses but not in a bibliography. If consulted online include a URL or database name and any identification number supplied or recommended by the database. To cite an abstract add the word “abstract.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished manuscript citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of unpublished manuscripts, like the titles of other unpublished works, appear in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the words unpublished manuscript and the date of the version consulted, if known; for electronic files, a last-saved or last-modified date may be appropriate. End the citation with an indication of format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectures, papers, and posters presented at meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: The sponsorship, location, and date of the meeting at which a speech was given or a paper, slides, or poster presented follow the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information is put in parentheses in a note but not in a bibliography. If available online include a URL. Papers in published proceedings may be treated as chapters or journal articles as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working papers and similar documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Working papers and similar documents can be treated in much the same way as a dissertation or thesis or as a lecture, paper, or other presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the term working paper is part of a formal series title, capitalize it. If the item is not available online it may be useful to add photocopy or otherwise indicate the form in which it may be consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private contracts, wills, and similar documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Private documents are occasionally cited in notes but rarely in bibliographies; more appropriately they are referred to in text (e.g., naming a will and date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalization is generally editorial discretion. Provide sufficient identifying data (e.g., registry numbers, proving dates) in notes as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlets, corporate reports, brochures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlets, corporate reports, brochures, and other freestanding publications are treated essentially as books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author and publisher data may not fit the normal pattern, but give sufficient information to identify the document; treat loose‑leaf service material similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript collections identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Full identification of most unpublished material usually requires giving the title and date of the item, series title (if applicable), name of the collection, and name of the depository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no general agreement on the sequence of elements beyond placing the cited item first in a note; whatever sequence is adopted should be used consistently. Citations of collections consulted online generally follow the same form with the addition of a URL or database name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes versus bibliography for manuscript collections
rubrics_metrics.description: In a note, the main element of a manuscript citation is usually a specific item and is thus cited first. In a bibliography, the main element is usually either the collection in which the specific item may be found, the author(s) of the items in the collection, or the depository for the collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries beginning with the name of the collection or the last name of the author tend to be easiest to locate in a bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to include specific items in bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific items are not included in a bibliography unless only one item from a collection is cited and is considered important enough to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise list the collection under its name or the author of the items contained therein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing letters and similar items in manuscript collections
rubrics_metrics.description: A note citation of a letter starts with the name of the letter writer, followed by to, followed by the name of the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given names may be omitted if identities are clear; identifying material may be added if appropriate. The word letter is usually omitted (understood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific versus generic titles for manuscript collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks are used only for specific titles (e.g., “Canoeing through Northern Minnesota”), but not for generic names such as report or minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic names are capitalized if part of a formal heading actually appearing on the manuscript, lowercased if merely descriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates format in manuscript citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of months may be spelled out or abbreviated, as long as done consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are many references to specific dates, the day-month-year form (8 May 1945) reduces clutter, though American month-day-year style (May 8, 1945) may be preferred; be consistent (see 6.38, 9.31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Folios, leaves, and page numbers for manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Older manuscripts are usually numbered by signatures only or by leaves (sometimes called folios) rather than by page. More recent ones usually carry page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the abbreviations p. and pp. if needed; leaves introduced at beginning or end when rebound are not usually counted. Some collections have identifying series or file numbers which may be included in a citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Papers' and 'manuscripts' terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles of manuscript collections, the terms papers and manuscripts are synonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are acceptable, as are the abbreviations MS and (pl.) MSS. Use TS to distinguish a typescript or computer printout from a handwritten document if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of depositories in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The location (city and state) of well-known depositories such as major university libraries is rarely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include location when helpful for identification of less-well-known repositories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short forms for subsequent manuscript citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of subsequent citations of other items in a cited manuscript collection (short forms) will vary according to the proximity of the earlier notes, the use of abbreviations, and other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute consistency may occasionally be sacrificed to readers’ convenience; choose clear short forms based on earlier full citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters in private collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters, memorandums, and such that have not been archived may be cited like other unpublished material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace repository information with wording such as “in the author’s possession” or “private collection,” and do not mention a location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing reference works in print
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known reference books (major dictionaries and encyclopedias) are normally cited in notes rather than bibliographies. For alphabetically arranged works cite the item (not the volume or page number) preceded by s.v. (sub verbo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a physical edition is cited specify the edition number (if not the first) and the date the volume or set was issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference works as bibliographic entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Most other reference works are more appropriately listed with full publication details like any other book resource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authored entries in reference works, cite individual entries by author as you would for a contribution to a multiauthor book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing online reference works
rubrics_metrics.description: Online reference works can be cited much like their printed antecedents; they are normally cited in the notes rather than in bibliographies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For continually updated resources include a posted publication or revision date; if none is available supply an access date. Include a URL as the last element. Time stamps may be included for frequently updated resources. Follow the usage in the source for author name inversion and formatting (cf. 14.206).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing individual reference entries by author
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference works with substantial, authored entries it may be appropriate to cite individual entries by author, much like contributions to a multiauthor book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such citations may be included in a bibliography when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing paintings, photographs, and sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about paintings, photographs, sculptures, or other works of art can usually be presented in the text rather than in a note or bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a note or bibliography entry is needed, list the artist, a title (in italics), and a date of creation or completion, followed by information about the medium and the location of the work. For works consulted online add a URL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition catalogs
rubrics_metrics.description: An exhibition catalog is often published as a book and is treated as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If space is tight add the phrase Exhibition catalog; include publisher and place as for a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about maps can usually be presented in the text rather than in a note or bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a note or bibliography entry is needed, list the cartographer (if known) and the title of the map (in italics) or a description (in roman), followed by the scale and size (if known) and publication details or location. Undated maps consulted online should include an access or revision date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible citations: chapter and verse format
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the Jewish or Christian scriptures usually appear in text citations or notes. Parenthetical or note references to the Bible should include book (in roman and usually abbreviated), chapter, and verse—never a page number. A colon is used between chapter and verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidance on when to abbreviate (see 10.44) and use full versions spelled out at first occurrence for general readers; specialists may use abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify version for scriptural citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Since books and numbering are not identical in different versions, it is essential to identify which version is being cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general readers spell out the version at first occurrence; for specialists abbreviations may be used throughout (see 10.48).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing other sacred works
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the sacred and revered works of other religious traditions may be treated in a manner similar to biblical or classical works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations of transliterated texts should indicate the name of the version or translator. The Koran is set in roman and citations use arabic numerals and colons (e.g., Koran 19:17-21); collective terms like Vedas or Upanishads are capitalized and set in roman, with particular parts italicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to cite classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical primary source references are ordinarily given in text or notes and are included in a bibliography only when the reference is to information or annotation supplied by a modern author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established conventions for numbering (books, sections, lines) which remain the same across editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying numbers in classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The numbers identifying the various parts of classical works—books, sections, lines, and so on—remain the same in all editions, whether in the original language or in translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Arabic numerals. Where letters also are used they are usually lowercased. Omit page numbers except for introductions, notes, and translations or modern editorial matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations in classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations of authors’ names and of works, collections, and so forth are used extensively in classical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard lists (e.g., Oxford Classical Dictionary). When abbreviations are used, use them rather than ibid. in succeeding references. Avoid abbreviations when only two letters are omitted or when more than one writer could be meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation conventions in classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma between the name of a classical author (abbreviated or not) and the title of a work. No punctuation intervenes between title and identifying number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical divisions are separated by periods with no space. Use commas between two or more references to the same source, semicolons between different sources, en dashes between continuing numbers. If bk. or sec. are needed, commas separate different elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing specific editions of classical works
rubrics_metrics.description: Details of the edition used, along with translator (if any) and the facts of publication, should be either specified the first time a classical work is cited or given elsewhere in the scholarly apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If several editions are used, the edition (or an abbreviation) should accompany each citation; in bibliographies provide full edition details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of classical works formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of works and published collections are italicized whether given in full or abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Latin and transliterated Greek titles are capitalized sentence-style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superscripts for edition numbers in classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: A superior figure is sometimes used immediately after the title of a work (or its abbreviation), and preceding any other punctuation, to indicate the number of the edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the superscript before punctuation that ends the title element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collections of inscriptions citation form
rubrics_metrics.description: Arabic numerals are used in references to volumes in collections of inscriptions; periods follow the volume and inscription numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further subdivisions are treated as in other classical references; some collections may be cited only by the name of the editor (no comma needed when editor stands for title).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing fragments of classical texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fragments are not uniformly numbered; they are published in collections and numbering is usually unique to an edition. Two numbers separated by a period usually indicate fragment and line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor’s name must follow the number. In citations of two or more editions either parentheses or an equals sign may be used to indicate equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern editions of classics
rubrics_metrics.description: When Greek, Latin, or medieval classics are cited by page number, the edition must be specified, and normal rules for citing books are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide editor and translator information and publication facts in the bibliography or first note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medieval references format
rubrics_metrics.description: The form for classical references may equally well be applied to medieval works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow classical-style numbering for divisions (book, chapter, line) and specify edition/translation where page numbers are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing classic English poems and plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic English poems and plays can often be cited by book, canto, and stanza; stanza and line; act, scene, and line; or similar divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication facts can be omitted when such divisions are used. For frequently cited works—especially Shakespeare—specify the edition in the first note reference or in the bibliography if page numbers are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short forms for classic English works
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation may be shortened by omitting act, line, and the like, as long as the system used has been explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arabic numerals are used, separated by periods. In immediately succeeding references it is usually safer to repeat all numbers. The author’s name may be omitted if clear from the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published musical scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Published musical scores are treated in much the same way as books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include composer/arranger, title (formating as for books), edition/series information, publisher, and date as appropriate.
